newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam's central bank bemoans investment dearth.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam's central bank bemoans investment dearth.

text.p: Vietnam's central bank chief, betraying concern that a dearth of domestic investment could choke off the country's rapid economic growth, has told National Assembly delegates that steps are needed to encourage borrowing.

The official Vietnam News on Thursday quoted State Bank of Vietnam governor Cao Sy Kiem as saying high interest rates and poor confidence in the local currency, the dong, had made business wary of borrowing for medium- and long-term investment.
Foreign investment, encouraged by a raft of market-style economic reforms, has flooded into the communist country in the past five years.

But domestic investment remains thin on the ground and economists say that unless there is an increase, Vietnamese industry could run into production bottlenecks and face problems tackling an already record trade deficit.
The ceiling on local currency loan rates has been slashed to 1.25 percent a month from 2.1 percent this year to boost growth and narrow the gap between dong and U.S. dollar rates.
"But the adjustment of interest rates was slow and some rates were still high," Kiem was quoted as saying.
He also told National Assembly delegates that too few enterprises had raised capital by selling shares and suggested that commercial banks should issue bonds and shares.

Fewer than a dozen of Vietnam's roughly 6,000 state-owned companies have sold shares to the public. Foreign bankers say the glacial pace of "equitisation" makes it unlikely that plans to set up a stock market will be implemented before the end of the century.
Kiem said the absence of a stock market was among an array of impediments to raising long-term investment capital.
